rows.question: I've just bought a used car. What do I need to do to tax it and get it registered in my name?

answer.answer:
Tax and registration steps for a used car you've just bought:

1. Get the paperwork from the seller. The seller should have the V5C log book and the green 'new keeper' slip. The seller usually registers the vehicle to you, either online or by post:
   - Online: the seller registers it to you online, fills in the green 'new keeper' slip and gives it to you, and destroys the V5C.
   - By post: the seller completes the relevant section of the V5C (section 2 for the new-style log book, or section 6 and the section 8 declaration for the older style, which you must also sign), gives you the green slip, and posts the V5C to DVLA.

2. Tax the vehicle straight away. You can't legally use a used vehicle on the road until it's taxed. Use the green 'new keeper' slip, or the V5C if it's already in your name, with the online service at gov.uk/vehicle-tax. You can also tax at a Post Office. Payment can be by Direct Debit, debit or credit card.

3. Check the new V5C when it arrives. It's your responsibility to check that all the details are correct.

If there's no V5C: DVLA advises not to buy a vehicle without one. If you still go ahead, send form V62 to DVLA to register it in your name, which costs £25. You can't tax it without a new keeper slip, so you'd need to apply for a new V5C by post (also £25 for the replacement) and can tax it at the same time.

If you're registering by post and the V5C hasn't arrived after 4 weeks, contact DVLA. If you need a V5C sent to you after the seller has posted it, use form V62 with the new keeper slip from the most recent V5C. Without that slip it costs £25.

I didn't find a deadline for notifying DVLA of the change of keeper in these pages, so check the registration guidance if you need one.

rows.question: I'm moving house. Which of my licence and vehicle records do I need to update?

answer.answer:
When you move house, update these with DVLA:

1. Driving licence: change the address on your full or provisional licence. This is free, and you can keep driving while you wait for the new licence. It usually arrives within 3 weeks by post. Apply online, or by post if you want to change your name at the same time.
2. Vehicle log book (V5C): change the address. This is usually free. Apply online, or by post by writing the new address in section 3 (new style log book) or section 6 (older style) and sending the whole log book to DVLA. Don't use a PO Box address. If you also need to change your name, or you're moving abroad, different rules apply.
3. Vehicle tax Direct Debit: update the address if you pay vehicle tax this way.
4. Personalised registration number document (V750 or V778): change the address if you have one.

You can be fined up to £1,000 if you don't tell DVLA when your address changes. If your vehicle is off the road, you can update the V5C address online and then register it as off the road (SORN).

The pages I found don't cover insurance, so check with your insurer separately.

rows.question: My car is over 40 years old. Does it need an MOT, and does it need vehicle tax?

answer.answer:
MOT: You don't need one if the car was built or first registered more than 40 years ago and no "substantial changes" (e.g. replacing the chassis, body, axles or engine in a way that changes how the vehicle works) have been made. You must still keep it roadworthy; using it in a dangerous condition can bring a fine of up to £2,500 and 3 penalty points.

Vehicle tax: You must still tax it, as driving an untaxed vehicle is illegal (£80 fine for not taxing on time). Whether you pay depends on build date: if built before 1 January 1986 (or, if build date unknown, first registered before 8 January 1986), you can apply to stop paying from 1 April 2026, though you still have to tax it. Later-built cars pay the normal rate. The exemption doesn't apply if the car is used for hire or reward or commercially.

To apply, take to a Post Office that handles vehicle tax: your V5C log book in your name, your V11 reminder letter if you have one, and evidence of MOT or MOT exemption (V112 if listed). If you lack the log book, apply for a V62 (£25 fee).

rows.question: I'm 17 and want to learn to drive. What licence and tests do I need, and what do they cost?

answer.answer:
You need a provisional driving licence, then a theory test and a practical driving test (for a car).

Licence: You can apply for a provisional licence from 15 years 9 months, and you can usually start driving a car at 17. Applying online costs £34 (by post, £43 with form D1). You must be able to read a number plate from 20 metres and have been given permission to live in Great Britain for at least 185 days.

Learning: You must be supervised. This can be an approved driving instructor or a qualified supervisor (aged 21+, with a full licence held for at least 3 years, qualified for the vehicle type). The car must display L plates, be taxed, and be insured for you as a learner. You can't use motorways unless you're with an approved driving instructor in a car with dual controls.

Tests (booked through GOV.UK):
- Theory test: £23 for a car.
- Practical driving test: £62 on weekdays, or £75 in the evening, at weekends or on bank holidays.

Costs from unofficial booking sites are usually higher. Lessons with an instructor are extra and set by the instructor.

rows.question: My car has been written off. What do I tell DVLA and what happens to my vehicle tax?

answer.answer:
Tell DVLA online at GOV.UK (Monday–Friday 7am–9pm, Saturday and Sunday 7am–8pm), or by post. Have ready: your insurance company's name and postcode (entered under 'provide trader details'), the vehicle registration number, and the 11-digit reference number from the yellow 'sell, transfer or part-exchange your vehicle to the motor trade' section of the V5C log book. Failing to tell DVLA can lead to a £1,000 fine. Before you finish, check the log book name and address are correct (apply by post if not), and remove any personalised registration number from the vehicle. Destroy the yellow section once finished; you don't send it to DVLA. Your insurer will ask for the rest of the log book (if they ask for the whole thing, write to DVLA with the insurer's details and the date you handed the car over).

Vehicle tax: DVLA cancels your vehicle tax once told. You get a refund for any full months left, sent as a letter/cheque to the name and address on the log book, calculated from the date DVLA receives your information. If you pay by Direct Debit, it is cancelled automatically. You won't get refunds for credit card fees, the 5% Direct Debit surcharge, or the 10% surcharge on a single 6-month payment.

rows.question: I'm over 70 and have a medical condition. How do I renew my driving licence?

answer.answer:
If you're 70 or over and have a medical condition, you renew your licence the same way as anyone aged 70+, but you must declare the condition in the application.

1. Use the online service if you can. You can renew online for free if you're 70 or over (or will be within 90 days), your licence has expired or expires within 90 days, you live in Great Britain (Northern Ireland has a separate service), you meet the minimum eyesight requirement, and you're not prevented from driving for any reason. You must renew every 3 years. Renewal by post is needed for a C1 or D1 entitlement.

2. Declare your condition. You must tell DVLA about notifiable conditions when you renew at 70 or over. You don't need to contact DVLA separately; the application form asks for this information. Notifiable conditions include things such as diabetes or insulin use, fainting (syncope), heart conditions, sleep apnoea, epilepsy, strokes and glaucoma. Failing to tell DVLA can lead to a fine of up to £1,000.

3. What happens next. DVLA may contact your doctor or consultant, arrange an examination, or ask you to take a driving assessment or eyesight or driving test. It may take longer if it's referred to a doctor. DVLA can decide that you need a new licence, grant a shorter licence (1, 2, 3 or 5 years), require adapted controls in your car, or tell you to stop driving and surrender your licence. If you're told to stop, you can send more medical evidence, reapply when the letter allows, or appeal (in England and Wales, to the magistrates' court within 6 months and tell DVLA in writing; in Scotland, to the sheriff's court within 21 days).

4. Driving while you wait. You can usually keep driving while DVLA considers your application if you have your doctor's support to keep driving, had a valid licence, drive only under the conditions of your previous licence, the application is less than a year old, your last licence wasn't revoked or refused for medical reasons, you're not disqualified, and you weren't disqualified as a high-risk offender on or after 1 June 2013. If your application has given you a medical decision in the form, follow the driving guidance in that form.

If you're unsure what to declare or what medical evidence to send, check with your doctor, or contact DVLA's Drivers Medical Group (Swansea, SA99 1DF) for advice.
